lessonTitle: Why corners make good features: the Harris response
md: Harris scores a window by how much it changes under shifts in every direction. Both eigenvalues of $M$ large means corner; that is what makes a point localizable in two dimensions.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: "No mutex in the code" does not make an algorithm lock-free. If one stalled thread can prevent all others from completing, it is blocking, even if it only uses atomic instructions. Michael and Scott call out published queues that are "lock-free but not non-blocking" for exactly this reason, and Vyukov says the same of their own bounded queue (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
md: Lock-free data structures are two problems: the CAS protocol that keeps the structure consistent, and the reclamation scheme that keeps removed nodes alive until no thread can still be reading them. Get both right, or use a library that has.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Why log at all, and why not log everything
md: The log you need is usually older than the moment you learn you need it. Decide what to collect and how long to keep it from the questions an investigation will ask, then pay for that deliberately.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Alert quality: precision, recall and the base-rate trap
md: Low precision does not just waste time; it trains people to ignore alerts. Target's alerts were real, but an alert stream that is usually wrong teaches analysts that the next one probably is too. Precision is a security property.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: With dynamic scaling the RoPE of every cached token changes when $s$ changes. The YaRN paper notes the correct implementation caches keys *before* applying RoPE; caching rotated keys silently mixes two different scalings.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Build it: YaRN tables and a four-host ring in NumPy
md: Both halves of the course fit in about 60 lines: the frequency table is a per-pair multiplier on inv_freq (check it against the library you serve with), and Ring Attention is an online-softmax merge over blocks in any order, with one masking rule per block: past blocks in full, the diagonal block causally, future blocks skipped.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Recurrent depth at scale: prelude, core block and coda
md: A looped model can quietly stop using its loop. If it learns to ignore $\mathbf{s}$, extra iterations do nothing. Track validation loss at several iteration counts (Huginn tracked 1, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64) during training, not just at the default.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
md: A d90 of 200 does not mean that 200 hand-picked weights would do. The 200 numbers are projected through a dense random map, so every original weight still moves a little. And 90% of full performance is the bar, not 100%.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Composing adapters: switching, merging and task arithmetic
md: Merging is not free. The TIES authors found sign conflicts even between just two models, growing with every model added, and every method here has knobs (weights, density, lambda) that change the result. Evaluate each task, and the base skills, after merging, and tune those knobs on held-out data.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Measuring forgetting: TOFU, MUSE and the forget-retain tradeoff
md: Unlearning is judged against the retrained model on two axes at once: forget metrics should match it (not undershoot it) and utility should stay near it. Under-unlearning and over-unlearning both leak that the data was there.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Code signing: what a signature on a Mac proves
md: A valid signature says *who* built the code and that it is unchanged. It does not say the code is safe. Attackers sign malware with Developer ID certificates obtained under real or stolen identities, and in the 3CX case (lesson 17) the vendor's own build system signed the trojanised app.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Hunting across a fleet: osquery tables and detection logic
md: Mac fleets are full of developers who run curl, shells and unsigned tools all day. Rules that fire on "osascript ran" drown a SOC. Anchor detections on combinations and ancestry (browser to Terminal to curl to osascript to dscl) and on things legitimate tools rarely do (validating a user's password from a script).

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: A safe analysis lab and the analysis workflow
md: Malware can notice it is in a VM and change behaviour (ATT&CK calls this Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, T1497). An empty or 'boring' run does not prove a file is benign; it may prove only that the sample saw your lab.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Command and control: beacons, jitter and Cobalt Strike
md: C2 detection rests on things the operator finds hard to change: timing patterns, the process making the connection, rare destinations, and on-host artifacts. Fortra's own guide shows the traffic shape can be reconfigured (Malleable C2 profiles let an operator change how Beacon's HTTP traffic looks), so content signatures alone age quickly.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: How rankings shift as you cut dimensions: Matryoshka vs standard
md: A good Matryoshka prefix gives a coarser version of the full ranking: close items blur together, but far items stay far. A standard model's prefix promises nothing; in the toy it gives a different, noisy ranking. That is why prefixes of a model trained for them are the safe choice for shortlisting.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule
md: Bubble = (p - 1) / (v m). 1F1B bounds activation memory to p microbatches; interleaving divides the bubble by v at the cost of v times more pipeline sends.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Measuring the result: MFU, HFU and what the numbers count
md: Do not compare a paper's achieved TFLOP/s across systems without checking what it counts. Narayanan et al.'s 52% includes recomputation FLOPs; PaLM introduced MFU precisely because HFU depends on implementation choices like rematerialization (another name for recomputation).

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Know normal: the process tree, command lines and the PEB
md: Kernel-side data (EPROCESS, and the VADs of the next lesson) is what the process cannot easily edit; user-side data (PEB, loader lists, command line) is what it can. When they disagree, believe the kernel side and ask why the user side was changed.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation
md: Fragmentation is not a leak. In a leak, *live* data grows because the program forgets to free. With fragmentation, live data is flat while the *footprint* grows. Tell them apart by comparing the bytes the allocator says are allocated with the memory it holds: a leak raises both, fragmentation widens the gap.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Relaxed: one agreed history per variable, nothing more
md: Myth: "Relaxed writes may take ages to show up, and SeqCst makes them visible sooner." The memory model says nothing about timing at all, only about order. A stronger ordering does not make data travel faster; it may even slow your program down.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
md: Holding a guard is holding back everyone's garbage. Pinning across a blocking call, a lock wait or a long iteration stops the epoch from advancing for all threads. crossbeam provides `Guard::repin` to briefly unpin and pin again inside long loops; references loaded before the repin are no longer protected.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Where things live: code, static data, heap and stack
md: The bug class tells you how memory is misused; the region tells you what gets damaged. Stack overflows threaten return addresses, heap overflows threaten neighbouring objects and allocator data.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
md: A subtle limit of contrastive loss: it pulls every same-identity pair toward distance 0, so it tries to squash all images of one person onto a single point. The authors of FaceNet (Google's 2015 face recognition system, next lesson) argued that a triplet loss is better suited, because it only asks same-identity images to be closer than other identities, letting one person's images spread out along a region.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: When the optimizer deletes the code you meant to time
md: Misconception: "returning or summing the result is enough". Using the output defeats dead-code elimination, but not constant folding. The input must also come from somewhere the compiler cannot see through. JMH's constant-folding sample says to read inputs from non-final fields of a state object, and warns against making them `final` even when your IDE suggests it.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
md: The Miles docs do not publish a line-by-line diff against slime. This course teaches what Miles documents and measures; do not conclude from it that slime lacks any particular feature.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Low-precision RL: formats, scales and the precision contract
md: TITO fixes which tokens are trained on, R3 fixes which experts process them, and the precision contract fixes how each matmul is quantized. Each removes one cause of the importance ratio drifting away from 1.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: LRB: learning to evict like a relaxed Belady
md: The **good decision ratio** (good evictions divided by all evictions) grades each eviction individually. The LRB authors found it correlates strongly with the final byte miss ratio, so they used it to choose features, model, loss and sizes from one simulation pass instead of hours-long full simulations per design.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Dynamic instrumentation with Frida: watch and change a running app
md: On a device its user controls, any value in the app's memory and any boolean the app computes can be read and changed. Design so that changing them gains nothing: keys in secure hardware, decisions on the server.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
md: The paper counts cache size in **elements**, regardless of storage precision. Quantizing the cache, storing each element in fewer bits such as FP8 (an 8-bit floating-point format) or lower, is a separate, stackable trick. When comparing headline numbers, check whether both sides use the same precision.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why MLA can beat GQA at equal cache, and converting models
md: At equal cache, GQA is MLA with selector up-projections, so MLA can only add expressiveness. Converting a trained model to MLA means confining RoPE to a small part, compressing the rest into a latent, and fine-tuning briefly.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Many GPUs, many tenants: placement, cold starts and fairness
md: Routing every request for an adapter to one GPU looks efficient, since fewer distinct adapters per batch means fewer bytes. Under skewed popularity it concentrates the hottest tenant on one replica. Replicate hot adapters, pin only the tail, and let migration or a load-aware dispatcher handle the rest.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
md: RRF rewards agreement between phrasings. A relevant document that only one phrasing finds stays low, and a junk document that two phrasings share can outrank it. That is why the quality of the phrasings matters as much as their number.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Common misconception: an MTP model does not have to emit several tokens per step. Gloeckle et al. use only the next-token head for ordinary decoding. The other heads are optional, and lesson 7 shows how they can be reused to draft tokens for faster decoding.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why orthogonalize: steepest descent under the spectral norm
md: Pick the ruler, get the optimizer. Frobenius gives gradient descent, the largest-entry norm gives sign descent (Adam without moving averages), the spectral norm gives the orthogonalized update. For a hidden linear layer the spectral norm is the one that bounds how much its outputs move.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
md: Do not judge an optimizer by a single untuned comparison. The Muon post argues that the most common reason optimizers that claimed to beat AdamW never caught on is an undertuned AdamW baseline, and proposes competitive benchmarks (like the NanoGPT speedrun record, where anyone can revert to AdamW) as the standard of evidence.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: The muP rules, layer by layer
md: Every piece is needed. Keeping $1/\sqrt{d}$ attention, using plain `torch.optim.Adam` instead of `MuAdam`, or forgetting to scale `d_ffn` along with `d_model` silently breaks transfer while the model still trains. Lesson 7 shows how to catch this.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: A lock is two things at once: mutual exclusion (one atomic read-modify-write decides a single winner) and visibility (Acquire on lock, Release on unlock, so each unlock happens-before the next lock).

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC is not the same as no locking. Two transactions that update the *same* row still conflict: the second one waits for the first to commit or roll back. MVCC only stops readers and writers from blocking each other.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
md: SSI = snapshot isolation plus non-blocking tracking of rw edges. It aborts a transaction in any dangerous structure, so every committed set is serializable; the application's job is to retry on 40001.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Why states hack: five purposes behind state operations
md: "It was a nation state, nothing could have stopped it" is a common excuse. Volt Typhoon relayed its traffic through old home and small-office routers that no longer received security updates, and many state intrusions start with known, unpatched flaws or stolen passwords. State backing buys patience and resources, not magic.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Pre-positioning: Volt Typhoon and access held for a crisis
md: Pre-positioning turns "detect and evict" into "detect, evict, and be ready to run without the network". If an advisory says an actor is positioned to disrupt, the response plan has to include continuity of the physical service, not only incident response on computers.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Picking blocks: importance scores come for free
md: Top-n selection itself is not differentiable, but NSA does not need it to be. The scores come from the compression branch, which is trained by the ordinary language modeling loss through its own output, and the selected tokens are trained through the selection branch's attention. No auxiliary loss is required.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
md: Global hashes, PDQ included, do poorly when one image is a **crop** of another; the PDQ document lists deep crops as out of scope. ImageHash's documentation shows how fast aHash degrades with rotation on its test image: 2 bits at 1 degree, 11 at 6 degrees, 21 at 26 degrees. Large borders, overlaid text and memes also defeat them.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Where the attacker stands: on-path, off-path and on your LAN
md: Know the position before you pick the defence. Encryption (TLS) defeats on-path reading and rewriting of content. Unpredictable numbers (random ports, sequence numbers, IDs) defeat off-path guessing. Switch features such as MAC limiting, DHCP snooping and ARP inspection stop local attackers from becoming on-path.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Flooding DNS and HTTP/2: Dyn 2016 and Rapid Reset 2023
md: Application-layer floods win through asymmetry: a cheap action for the client (open and cancel a stream) that is expensive for the server. Defences measure behaviour per connection and close abusive connections outright, because per-request blocking leaves the cheap channel open. The pattern recurs: MadeYouReset (CVE-2025-8671, 2025) uses malformed control frames to make the server reset streams itself.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Zeek's protocol logs and pivoting with uid, fuid and Community ID
md: Two IDs carry most investigations: Zeek's uid joins logs about one connection, fuid joins logs about one file. Community ID extends the join to other tools. Learn to move between them quickly; it is most of the job.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Network forensics for incident response: a worked IcedID investigation
md: Capture and analyse only traffic you own or are authorised to monitor. Practice pcaps of real infections contain working malware and sometimes real personal data from the lab: open them on an isolated, non-Windows machine and never run extracted files.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Ports, sockets and NAT
md: NAT is not a firewall. It drops unsolicited inbound packets only as a side effect of having no table entry. Port-forwarding rules, devices that open forwards automatically, IPv6 (often no NAT at all) and connections started from inside all bypass that "protection". Use an actual firewall policy.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
md: malloc chooses addresses, the first write chooses the node. Initialize data in parallel with the same pinned threads and the same partitioning that will later use it.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Wear leveling, TRIM, hot and cold data, endurance
md: Lifetime and throughput both scale with 1/A. The levers to lower A are all about making victim blocks emptier: more spare, TRIM of dead data, writes that are large and sequential, and grouping data that will die at the same time.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Training and tuning a detector in practice
md: The AP number picks the model; the confidence threshold, chosen on validation data that looks like deployment, decides how it behaves.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
md: The shape of the data decides which questions you can ask. Metrics answer "how often, how slow, for everyone". Traces answer "where did the time go inside this one request". Logs answer "what exactly happened at this instant".

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
md: A dashboard is an ordered list of questions, not a list of metrics. Start with the SLO burn rate (are users hurt), then symptoms (what is broken), then causes and changes (why), then one link into a single trace (prove it).

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Judging answers on documents with ANLS
md: ANLS = average over questions of the best (1 minus normalized edit distance) against any ground truth, zeroed when the distance reaches 0.5. It rewards nearly right reading, not semantic equivalence.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Privilege separation: OpenSSH's design case
md: Privilege separation protects only the code that was moved into the unprivileged half. regreSSHion (CVE-2024-6387, covered in linux-for-security) was a signal-handler race in sshd's privileged code which, in Qualys's words, "is not sandboxed and runs with full privileges". That is why OpenSSH keeps shrinking the privileged parts: the 9.8 and 10.0 splits move more code out of them.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Ethics and law first: public is not the same as permitted
md: Ask legal, authorised, ethical before every task. Public data is still personal data; combining it can create a harm none of the pieces had alone.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Verifying images and claims: provenance, reposts and hashes
md: Ask where and when an image first appeared before asking whether it was edited. Perceptual hashes find reposts; provenance and corroboration decide the claim.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: People-search sites, data brokers and protecting your own footprint
md: Understand the people-data industry so you can defend against it: brokers sell profiles, attackers use them, and you shrink exposure with settings, separation, MFA and removal requests.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CUDA builds: PTX, cubins and the architecture list
md: Cubins run only on the same major CC with an equal or higher minor; PTX JIT compiles forward to any equal or higher CC. Ship cubins for the GPUs you target plus PTX for the newest one, and keep the list short for development builds, because every entry multiplies CUDA compile time.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Flaky means uncontrolled state. Reproduce with the exact node id, order seed and loop count, find the state, and control it with a fixture. Reruns and quarantine are temporary and cost real signal.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: Whatever the tool, the author's loop is the same: answer every comment, change the code where the reviewer was right, record what changed between versions, and carry earned review credit forward only while it still applies.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
md: Misconception: "syncing my fork" updates my laptop. GitHub's Sync fork button updates the fork on GitHub; `git fetch upstream` plus a merge updates your local copy. GitHub's docs point out that syncing locally does not update the fork on GitHub until you push. They are separate repositories.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
md: Misconception: `-s` signs the commit. It does not. `-s` (lowercase) adds a Signed-off-by text trailer, a legal statement. `-S` (uppercase, `--gpg-sign`) adds a cryptographic signature made with your private key, by default through GPG (GNU Privacy Guard), that GitHub can show as Verified. A project may require either, both, or neither.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: Outbound is what users get; inbound is what the project gets from you. Inbound=outbound needs no paperwork; a CLA is a one-time signed grant, often with an explicit patent license and a statement about your employer.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Reporting honestly: geomeans, many benchmarks and costs
md: Do not cherry-pick. Quoting only the best benchmark, dropping a regressed one, or rerunning until a borderline result flips are all ways to make noise look like a win. Reviewers who rerun your commands will find out.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A screenshot of a traceback is not complete. The maintainer cannot search it, copy the line numbers, or paste it into a test. Stack Overflow's guide says plainly: do not use images of code; paste text.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
md: The right size for a PR is **one self-contained change**: it does one thing, includes its tests, and leaves the system working. Line counts are a symptom; focus is the goal.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Recap: why the vLLM paper paged the KV cache
md: Knowing the exact output length would not fix this. Orca (Oracle) assumes perfect knowledge and still stores real token states in only 38.2% of KV memory, because contiguous chunks of different sizes still fragment the space and still cannot be shared.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Prefill on top of a cached prefix, and sharing the compute too
md: A common misconception: "the prefix is shared, so it is cheap to decode against". Block sharing saves storage and prefill compute. Decode traffic only drops when the kernel batches the queries that read the shared blocks, as cascade attention does.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: When authorisation is unclear: the Iowa courthouse arrests
md: Ambiguity is what got two professionals arrested. Write down: who owns each target, who signed for it, when testing may happen, who outside the client has been told, and two 24/7 ways to reach someone who can confirm it.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Why profilers sample stacks instead of timing every call
md: A sampling profiler answers one question: what fraction of CPU samples had this function on the stack? It is cheap because work happens per sample, not per call, and it is approximate because it is a sample.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
md: Common misconception: "unflushed stores are lost on a crash." Some are, some are not, and the hardware chooses. Treat each dirty cache line as independently maybe-persisted. Flushes give you a lower bound on what is durable, never an upper bound.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Envelope, header and display name: why spoofing works
md: Authentication checks answer "was this domain's use authorised?", never "is this message honest?". A display-name spoof or lookalike domain passes them cleanly. Defences need both: DMARC against exact-domain spoofing, and human-facing cues plus process rules for the rest.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
md: Two rules give every struct layout: **each field's offset is a multiple of its alignment**, and **the struct's size is a multiple of its own alignment** (the largest field alignment). Everything else, including all the padding, follows from these.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
md: A top-down pose model inherits every mistake of its detector. If two people overlap and NMS merges their boxes, or the detector misses someone, the keypoint network has no way to recover that person. The authors of OpenPose, the bottom-up system in lesson 3, call this **early commitment**: the pipeline commits to the detector's boxes before it has looked at a single joint.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Five families, one competition and two spectacular breaks
md: Misconception: "an algorithm is quantum-safe until someone builds a quantum computer that breaks it." Both 2022 breaks ran on ordinary computers. Confidence in ML-KEM and ML-DSA comes from years of public cryptanalysis of lattice problems, and NIST still hedged with HQC, which it says is based on different math than ML-KEM.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
md: Post-filtering leaves the index untouched and is cheap when $s$ is large, but the result count is a random variable. To hold k results you must fetch on the order of $k/s$ candidates, and noticeably more for a high-probability guarantee.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Multi-tenancy: partition, shard or filter
md: The tenant filter is a selectivity distribution, not one number. Small tenants want exact scans, large ones want their own graph, and the shared graph with a filter only fits the middle. Tiered layouts exist because real tenant sizes are skewed.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Linking attacks: ZIP code, birth date and sex
md: Removing direct identifiers is not anonymisation. The GDPR's test (Recital 26) is whether anyone could identify a person with means reasonably likely to be used, and a twenty-dollar voter list was enough in 1997.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: When k-anonymity fails: l-diversity and t-closeness
md: k-anonymity protects against finding a row; l-diversity against learning a value because a class is uniform; t-closeness against a class whose distribution differs from the population. All are properties of a table, not of the process, which is the gap differential privacy fills.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Case: the 2020 US Census adopts differential privacy
md: Many accurate statistics from one dataset can reconstruct it (Dinur and Nissim's result, the Fundamental Law of Information Recovery). The 2020 Census answered with a public, budgeted epsilon instead of secret swapping, trading some accuracy for a guarantee that can be reasoned about.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Data protection impact assessments that change the design
md: DPIA: required before likely high-risk processing (GDPR Art. 35; WP248: two of nine criteria usually means yes). It must describe the processing, test necessity and proportionality, assess risks to people and record measures; unmitigated high risk goes to the regulator first (Art. 36).

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Credentials are the real currency: where they live on a host
md: Misconception: "we have MFA, so stolen hashes and tickets don't matter." Multi-factor authentication protects the sign-in that asks for it, usually remote access and cloud portals. Inside a Windows network, NTLM and Kerberos authentication to a file server or another workstation uses the hash or ticket directly and does not prompt for a second factor.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: What should a step reward measure? Value, progress, implicit PRMs
md: An implicit PRM's step reward is a difference of soft Q values under the *reference* model's continuations, learned from outcome labels. It is not a human judgement of the step, and like MC labels it measures how a step changes the expected outcome, not whether the step is mathematically valid.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: A process's life: exec, exit, wait, zombies and orphans
md: A process's life is fork, exec, exit, wait. Every child must be reaped by its parent or by whoever adopts it, or it stays a zombie. And in a threaded program, a forked child should do nothing but async-signal-safe calls until it execs.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Training per-slice codebooks and encoding a vector
md: Common misconception: a PQ code is a lossless compression of the vector. It is not. Two different vectors with the same code are indistinguishable to the index, and every distance computed from codes inherits the quantization error.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned prompts are brittle
md: Misconception: "a prompt that works is a good prompt". A hand-tuned prompt is fitted to one model, one task and the handful of examples you looked at. Change the model, the data or even the separator characters and the ranking of prompts can change.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Self-consistency grades a generator with a predictor that was trained on natural proteins, and both can be wrong in the same direction. A design that AF2 loves is not proven to fold: it has passed one cheap filter. Everything after this point costs money and weeks.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Reading CSV exports and JSON records without breaking them
md: Never split CSV or JSON by hand. `csv.DictReader` and `json.loads` implement the quoting and escaping rules you would otherwise get wrong, and wrong parsing in security tooling means missed indicators.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Vocabulary mismatch: why BM25 misses relevant documents
md: Better scoring cannot fix a zero-overlap miss. Query expansion changes **which documents can match at all** by adding terms to the query (or, in document expansion, to the documents). That is a recall tool first, and every added term is also a new way to match the wrong document.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: LLM expansion prompts, and deciding per query whether to expand
md: Treat expansion as a per-query risk. Report wins and losses next to the mean, keep the original query in every expanded query (repetition, weights or an original query weight), and switch expansion off for queries whose exact wording is the point.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
md: RaBitQ indexing: center and normalize, apply one random rotation, store the sign bits plus two floats per vector. The codebook is the rotated hypercube, so no k-means training is needed.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Business logic flaws: when correct code does the wrong thing
md: A logic flaw is an assumption the server never checks. To find one, list what the design assumes about users (what they send, in what order, how fast, how many accounts) and ask which assumption would pay them to break.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Limit overrun: one coupon, one balance, many parallel requests
md: Claim-first works only because the Set lives in this one process. Run two Node processes, or two servers, or keep the state in a real database, and the check and the claim are separate network calls again. The durable fix puts the claim where the state is: a unique constraint or a conditional update in the database (lesson 9).

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Hidden sub-states: Kettle's GitLab email race (CVE-2022-4037)
md: Every request is a sequence of steps, so every endpoint that edits shared state has sub-states. Decide each security-relevant value once, carry it with the work, and make the state change atomic, rather than writing a value early and reading it back later.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft safety: the election restriction and the Figure 8 trap
md: A Raft leader commits by counting replicas **only** for entries from its own current term. Older entries become committed indirectly, when a later current-term entry after them commits. Entries keep their original term number forever, which is why this rule is needed.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Query-document features: BM25 per field, coverage, proximity
md: Per-field BM25 features are not BM25F. BM25F (the subject of Elasticsearch's `combined_fields` query) merges term frequencies across fields before saturating. Separate per-field features saturate each field on its own and let the model weigh them. Both are useful; they are different numbers.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Three runs, seven verdicts: when metrics disagree
md: Disagreement between metrics is information, not noise. If binary metrics and exponential nDCG disagree, your system is trading coverage of relevant documents against putting the very best one first. Report at least one metric of each kind and say which user you care about.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Case: Kaseya VSA and REvil, July 2021: one tool, many victims
md: Any tool that can run code on many machines (RMM, patch management, EDR consoles, software deployment) is Tier 0. Keep it off the internet, behind MFA and a dedicated admin network, and watch it as closely as a domain controller. CISA's MSP guidance adds: MSP accounts out of admin groups, a dedicated VPN for MSP traffic, and the MSP's activity logged into the customer's own monitoring.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Two-sided SEND versus one-sided READ, WRITE and atomics
md: Polling the trailer only works if the NIC writes the message in increasing address order. FaRM notes that many NICs, including theirs, guarantee this for RDMA writes but not reads. It is a hardware property, not a verbs promise: registering memory with `IBV_ACCESS_RELAXED_ORDERING` explicitly gives up write-after-write ordering.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
md: Interpolation is not prediction. It never invents a position: it only blends two snapshots the server really sent. The cost is that every remote entity is shown late by the buffer delay, which is why aiming needs lag compensation.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
md: Space2 was shown only 23 times in 2000, although it is mobile users' second choice (0.25). Optimism-based exploration stops exploring once an arm looks clearly worse than the leader; that is the point, but it means some items get little data. Freshness boosts or explicit exploration slots are common additions.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Three ways to join two tables
md: Nested loop: cost about outer x inner-scan, works for any condition, great with an inner index and few outer rows. Merge join: one pass over each sorted input, needs sorted inputs and an equality key. Hash join: one pass over each input, needs an equality key and memory for the build side.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leaderless quorums: why R + W > N makes reads overlap writes
md: $R + W > N$ is a counting argument, nothing more: if the write really sits on W of the N designated replicas and the read really asks R of those same N, they share a replica. Lesson 4 shows how failures quietly break the "same N" part.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: KL regularization: a leash, not a cure
md: KL regularization and early stopping limit the *amount* of optimization, which keeps you on the rising side of the Goodhart curve. They cannot tell a good high-reward behavior from a bad one. Only a better reward, a conservative reward, or an outside check can do that.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Governance, risk and compliance: three jobs and who decides
md: Governance decides who decides. Risk management decides what is worth doing. Compliance proves to outsiders that you did what you are obliged to do. They overlap, but a company can be compliant and still badly governed, or well governed and still breached.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Security economics: how much to spend (the Gordon-Loeb model)
md: Gordon-Loeb's lessons for engineers: spend where a dollar reduces the most expected loss, not where the scariest weakness is; for the paper's broad families of breach functions the optimum is at most about 37 percent of expected loss; and making controls more effective beats making budgets bigger.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: One control, many frameworks: CIS Controls, HIPAA and the crosswalk
md: Do not run one programme per framework. Write each control once, build it to the strictest applicable requirement, map it to every framework it satisfies, and attach evidence that is collected automatically. Start from CIS IG1 if you have nothing; use the crosswalk to answer everyone else.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
md: Insurance does not replace controls or accountability. Regulators still fine you, customers still leave, and a claim can fail if your application overstated your controls or the event falls under an exclusion. Treat the policy wording as a contract engineers should read: what counts as a covered event, which notice deadlines apply, which incident responders you must use.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Colocated or disaggregated: where the engines live
md: Colocation trades memory and switch time for zero idle pools. Disaggregation trades network sync and staleness for overlap and freedom to size each pool. The long tail pushes large reasoning runs toward disaggregated, asynchronous designs.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Multi-turn agentic rollouts: tools, servers and token-in, token-out
md: A common misconception is that storing the chat transcript is enough, because the trainer can tokenize it again. Tokenizing is not the inverse of sampling: the policy may have sampled a non-canonical split, and tool parsers edit messages. Train on the ids the engine returned.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items
md: "The root cause" is usually a decision about where to stop asking, not a fact. The SRE book is careful here: systems are complex, and it is likely that multiple factors, each individually not the cause, are jointly causes. Its template says Root Causes, plural. Note that a cause chain pointing at a person is a sign you stopped one question early.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: When score fusion beats RRF
md: RRF trades information for robustness: it ignores how far apart scores are, so it cannot be fooled by scale, but it also cannot use a confident gap. With labels and comparable scores, a tuned convex combination usually wins; without them, RRF is the safe default.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Locks and refcounts as types: Guard, Opaque and Arc
md: The pattern is always the same: an `unsafe` C protocol (lock and unlock, get and put, register and unregister) becomes a value whose constructor does the first half and whose `Drop` does the second. The type system then tracks the protocol for every caller.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
md: A CPU only ever runs tasks from its own local DSQ. Everything else (global DSQ, custom DSQs, BPF maps) is staging. The pick order is local, then global, then `ops.dispatch()`.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Placement and preemption: idle CPUs, kicks, LOCAL_ON and locality
md: Placement is decided when a task lands in a local DSQ. `select_cpu` and the idle cpumask choose where, `LOCAL_ON` puts it there from any CPU, and kicks (`IDLE`, `PREEMPT`) decide when that CPU looks.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Secrets: what they are, how long they live, why they sprawl
md: A secret's danger is what it opens, times how long it works, times how many places it lives. Every technique in this course shrinks one of those three: least privilege shrinks the first, rotation and dynamic secrets the second, vaults and scanning the third.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: The end state: workload identity instead of stored secrets
md: The best secret is one that does not exist at rest. Where one must exist, make it short-lived, unique to one consumer, held in one audited place and rotated automatically with overlap.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: JavaScript: prototype pollution and code built from strings
md: Any code that writes `obj[key] = value` with a key from input, or walks nested input recursively, must refuse `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype`, or use objects with no prototype. Any string that reaches eval, Function or a string timer is code injection.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Compiler warnings and hardening flags a C reviewer should demand
md: Warnings find bugs; hardening flags limit the damage of the bugs you missed. Review build files like code: a change that removes either, or adds -Wno-format-security or -fno-stack-protector, needs the same scrutiny as a change to authentication.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IPsec building blocks: SAs, SPIs, ESP, AH and two modes
md: A common misconception: tunnel mode is not more encrypted than transport mode. Both use the same ESP encryption. Tunnel mode additionally hides the inner addresses and lets a gateway protect traffic for a whole network; transport mode is for two hosts protecting their own traffic.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Encrypting email itself: S/MIME, OpenPGP and EFAIL (2018)
md: EFAIL's root cause was releasing unauthenticated plaintext into an active renderer (HTML that fetches URLs). Authenticated encryption plus a strict rule (verify first, show nothing on failure) removes the gadget attack; disabling remote content in the client removes the easiest exfiltration channel.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Inside BeyondCorp: inventory, trust tiers and the access proxy
md: In an access-proxy design the device inventory and the identity system are part of the trusted computing base. If the inventory says a stolen laptop is healthy, every check downstream agrees.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: From a script to a pipeline: the parts of a security automation
md: A security automation is a small distributed system that holds powerful credentials and processes data attackers can influence. Design for duplicates, partial failure and hostile input from the first version.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Measuring AI triage: golden sets, precision, recall and attack success
md: Golden-set labels must come from completed investigations. If you label with first-look verdicts, you measure how well the model copies hurried humans, including their misses.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who attacks and why: criminals, states, insiders, activists
md: Ask "who would want this asset, and what would they do with it?" Criminals want quick money and reuse easy entry points such as stolen passwords. States want long, quiet access. Insiders already have access. The defence emphasis differs for each, but removing unused access helps against all of them.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
md: Kill chain: seven phases, and breaking any link stops the intrusion. ATT&CK: tactics (why) and techniques (how) with IDs, the shared language of detection rules and threat reports.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Building a programme from zero: the first 90 days
md: Inventory and owners first, then cheap actions that remove whole classes of risk, then a written strategy and budget built on what you found. Tools come after you know what they will watch and who will respond.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Reporting to the board: oversight duties and the annual cycle
md: A board is not an operations audience. Pages of vulnerability counts, tool names or "attacks blocked" give directors nothing to oversee and can later read as a CISO who never explained the real risk. Equally, never let the pack say something rosier than the internal record (lesson 15).

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Rebuilding after failure: Equifax, Maersk and Microsoft
md: Rebuilds that last change who leads and to whom they report, what leaders are rewarded for, how often the board looks, and what the company says publicly, not only how much it spends.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Presenting to a board: risk, money and decisions
md: Do not present fear or vanity. Breach headlines from other companies and "millions of attacks blocked" both waste the board's attention. Directors respond to clear risk, honest measures and a specific ask, and they remember who was straight with them.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting
md: A self-improvement loop is only as good as its filter. The precision of the check sets the quality of the kept data, and the set of problems the model can sometimes solve sets how far the loop can reach.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: What is safe to cache: scoping, context and invalidation
md: Never let the cache cross users for answers that depend on who is asking: balances, orders, permissions, anything personal. A false hit there is not a quality bug; it is a data leak. Scope by user or tenant, or bypass the cache for those requests entirely.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Validating outbound URLs in code
md: Validate the *destination*, not the *string*: fixed scheme, allowlisted host, resolved IP checked against private ranges, the connection pinned to that IP, and no automatic redirects. Then assume the check will one day fail and limit what the network lets the server reach.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: HiCache: a radix tree that spans GPU, host memory and storage
md: Misconception: "a large `--hicache-ratio` pools the host memory of all my servers." It only makes each instance's own L2 bigger. Cross-instance reuse needs a shared L3 backend, and the router must still send related requests where the KV is cheapest to reach.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Turning a road map into a weighted directed graph
md: A road network is a large, sparse, directed graph with **nonnegative** weights. Every fast routing algorithm in this course depends on the weights never being negative.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The DFT: one dot product per complex sinusoid
md: The DFT is a matrix-vector product: $N$ dot products of the signal with orthogonal complex sinusoids. Each $X[k]$ says how much of frequency $k$ is present (magnitude) and where it starts (phase), and the inverse DFT rebuilds $x$ exactly.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
md: Misconception: "my SIMD loop is slow, so I need wider vectors." If it streams from DRAM with little math per byte, it is memory-bound and AVX-512 will not help. Measure bytes per second against your machine's bandwidth first.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The buddy allocator: split in halves, merge with one XOR
md: Buddy trades internal fragmentation (power-of-two rounding, up to about 50 percent) for fast, simple coalescing: the buddy is one XOR away. It suits page-granular, physically contiguous memory, which is why Linux uses it for its page allocator and builds smaller allocators on top.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Low-precision rollout: FP8 weights, FP8 KV cache and INT4
md: Low precision in slime is a rollout-side copy: train in bf16, serve FP8 from a converted checkpoint whose `quantization_config` the trainer reuses at every sync. The price is that SGLang now samples from a rounded policy, a gap between rollout and trainer probabilities that lesson 8 measures and corrects.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Is the run working? Evaluation, metrics, checkpoints and recovery
md: Recovery has limits. Without straw or rollout dumps you keep the engines but cannot replay batches after the last checkpoint. If the ServingCluster actor or the whole Ray cluster is lost, you start serving again and resume from the checkpoint; node loss and preemption need your scheduler's help. A resume with a different TP or PP layout reinitializes RNG, so it is not bitwise identical.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: A toy chain in Python, and thinking in invariants
md: Before reading any contract, write down its invariants: "holds at least what it owes", "total shares match total assets", "only the owner can change the owner". Every bug class that follows is a way to break one of them.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The alert lifecycle, and why the queue is not first come, first served
md: Allow-listing the scanner fixes the noise but creates a blind spot: an attacker on that address is now invisible to the rule. The NCSC says allow lists must be "strongly object/time bounded" (one address, its scheduled window, an expiry date) "to minimise the risk of perpetual allow listing and the evasion of monitoring".

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Cloud key misuse, and what Snowflake customers could see in 2024
md: Cloud and SaaS triage starts with three questions: what kind of credential is this, where is it being used from compared with normal, and what did it touch. The third question can only be answered if the right logs (S3 data events, the warehouse's query history) were switched on and kept long enough before the incident.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Password and MFA friction: rules that backfire and rules that work
md: Misconception: "more password rules means more security". Composition rules and forced changes make people choose predictable variants and write them down. Length, a blocklist, rate limiting, and MFA that is bound to the site do the real work.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Testing the people layer: rules of engagement, ethics and metrics
md: Test processes, not people. Authorise every site with whoever controls it, plan for police, review lures for harm, report without names, and measure reporting speed and procedure compliance rather than click counts.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
md: A latent dying is not the same as a feature being absent from the model. It only means this SAE found no use for that column, often because of optimisation, not because the concept is missing.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
md: Every interpolator here is a weighted average $\sum_i \lambda_i z_i$. The only question is how to pick the weights. Keep this frame: the rest of the course compares weight recipes on the same six sensors.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
md: Kriging is the best linear unbiased predictor (linear: a weighted sum of readings; unbiased: weights sum to 1; best: smallest error variance) only under its own model. With few points, an unreliable variogram can make it worse than IDW, as in this toy. Its variance map is only as trustworthy as the variogram, so check calibration with standardized LOO errors.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts and prompt lookup decoding
md: All variants share one loop: draft cheaply (small model, extra heads, feature-level head, or string lookup), verify a chain or tree in one target pass, keep the accepted prefix plus one target token. They differ only in how they guess, and that sets alpha and c.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
md: Silence is where a language-model decoder is least constrained by audio. Short clips are padded to 30 s, long pauses leave long stretches of nothing, and the decoder can fill them with plausible web-caption text. The repetition and confidence checks do not catch a fluent, confident invented sentence.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Beyond the basic chunk: size classes, thread caches and fragmentation
md: Thread caches are a memory-for-speed trade. jemalloc's manual says it plainly: caching makes allocation very fast but increases memory use and fragmentation, since some objects stay parked in each thread's cache. TCMalloc moved to per-CPU caches because per-thread caches made footprint grow with the number of threads.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: When RAM runs out: page cache, file mappings, swap and thrashing
md: Little free memory is not a problem by itself. The page cache deliberately fills idle RAM with file data, and clean cached pages are reclaimable at any moment. Trouble shows up as rates: sustained swap-in and swap-out in `vmstat`, major faults per second, and processes stalled in direct reclaim.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
md: Window by **event time** (when the device measured) whenever the result should describe the physical world. Processing time describes your pipeline, not your sensor: a network hiccup would change a temperature average.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
md: Misconception: "QoS 2 at the device makes the pipeline exactly-once". MQTT QoS covers one hop. The bridge, Kafka producer, stream job and sink each need their own guarantee, and a single at-least-once hop reintroduces duplicates.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding and the full encoder-decoder stack
md: "Attention is all you need" does not mean attention is all there is. Without the FFN, residual connections, normalization and positional encodings, a stack of attention layers loses most of its parameters, its sense of order, and its trainability.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Term-frequency saturation: what k1 controls
md: Saturation does not mean repeated terms are ignored. With k1 = 1.2, going from 1 to 2 occurrences still raises the factor from 0.45 to 0.62. It means each extra occurrence is worth less than the one before, with a hard ceiling.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Which BM25? Variants, library differences and what they change
md: BM25 is a family: IDF form, (k1 + 1) scaling, length encoding and lower bounds vary. Measured differences between variants are small; parameter and analysis choices dominate. State all of them when you report a BM25 baseline.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
md: The training loop is the generic one (forward, cross-entropy, backward, clip, AdamW step), and the GPT-specific knowledge is in the settings: small normal init with scaled residual projections, decoupled weight decay on matrices only, warmup then cosine decay, and big token batches via gradient accumulation.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Integrals: accumulated change and area under a curve
md: An integral adds up infinitely many thin slices $f(x)\,dx$. To evaluate one, find an antiderivative and subtract its values at the ends; when no antiderivative is available, add up trapezoids numerically.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Jacobians: derivatives of vector-valued functions
md: The Jacobian generalizes the derivative to vector outputs, and the chain rule becomes a product of Jacobians. Backprop never forms those matrices: it carries one row (the loss gradient) backward and multiplies it into each layer's Jacobian, giving $W^\top$ products for inputs and outer products for weights.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Writing scripts: arguments, tests, if, loops and functions
md: `if`, `while`, `&&` and `||` all branch on an exit status. `[` and `test` are commands that turn a comparison into a status. Functions return a status with `return` and data on standard output.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Job control and signals: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, background jobs and trap
md: Reaching for `kill -9` first is a habit worth breaking. SIGKILL gives the program no chance to flush buffered output, remove lock or temporary files, or stop its own child processes, which can be left running as orphans. Send SIGTERM, give it a few seconds, then escalate.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
md: Static word embeddings (one fixed vector per word, whatever the sentence) encode co-occurrence statistics. Similar vectors mean *used in similar contexts*, which often but not always means *similar meaning*: antonyms like hot and cold share many contexts too.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
md: Prefill is math-bound (many tokens share each weight read). Decode is memory-bound (one token per weight read). Most GPU time in a long answer goes to decode, and the floor for each decode step is weight bytes divided by bandwidth.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: When one GPU is not enough: tensor parallelism and the decode floor
md: More GPUs do not automatically mean lower latency. Pipeline and data parallelism add capacity and throughput but leave single-request latency where it was, and tensor parallelism hits a floor set by per-layer communication latency.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
md: Control flow is the program counter. Straight-line code advances it by the instruction length; `jmp`, conditional jumps, `call` and `ret` overwrite it. A C `for` loop compiles to a compare plus a conditional jump backwards.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why real CPUs beat the simple loop: pipelines and prediction
md: Pipelining raises throughput, not the speed of any single instruction. The flow breaks on dependencies on recent results and on jumps the predictor gets wrong; a misprediction costs roughly the pipeline's length in cycles.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
md: SFT does not add much new knowledge. If the base model does not know a fact, a demonstration that states it mostly teaches the model to answer confidently in that style, which can increase made-up answers on other questions ([Gekhman et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05904)).

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
md: An inverted index maps each term to a sorted list of the documents that contain it. A query reads only the postings of its own terms, so the work depends on how common those terms are, not on how big the whole collection is.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Phrase and proximity queries with a positional index
md: Dropping stop words at index time breaks phrases made of them (*to be or not to be*, *The Who*). Lucene keeps a gap in the positions where a stop word was removed, so distances stay right, but the stop word itself can no longer be matched.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: C in one sitting: types, operators, control flow and functions
md: `sum / 10` with an int sum is integer division: 38, not 38.5. Convert one operand first, `(double)sum / 10`. A *cast* `(type)expr` converts a value to the named type.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
md: Off by one is the classic C bug: `for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) a[i] = 0;` writes a[n], one element past the end. The loop condition for an n-element array is `i < n`. Neither the compiler nor the CPU checks array bounds for you.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Function pointers and void *: writing generic code like qsort
md: qsort passes pointers **to elements**, not the elements. For an array of `item`, each argument is really an `item *`. For an array of strings declared `const char *words[]`, each element is itself a pointer, so the argument is a pointer to a pointer: `strcmp(*(const char * const *)a, *(const char * const *)b)`. Casting to the wrong type compiles silently and compares garbage.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Rust for C programmers: cargo, let, structs, enums and match
md: Rust's types carry what C leaves to convention: `Option<T>` instead of NULL, `Result<T, E>` instead of -1 and errno, exhaustive `match` so no case is forgotten, and `let` immutable unless you write `mut`. Ownership, next, does the same for *who frees this*.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Ownership in methods and loops: self, &self, &mut self and for
md: `.clone()` makes most of these errors disappear, but for E0507 a borrow (`&v[0]`) is usually what you meant. Clone only when you need an independent String that outlives the Vec or changes separately from it.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
md: Adding vectors of different dimensions is undefined in math. NumPy and PyTorch will sometimes *broadcast* (silently repeat) a smaller array to fit, so shape bugs can produce a result instead of an error. Always know the shape of every array you add. The tensors lesson gives the exact rule.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Determinant and inverse: undoing a map and solving Ax = b
md: A tiny determinant does not by itself mean trouble. $0.1I$ in 10 dimensions has determinant $10^{-10}$ yet condition number 1: it shrinks every direction equally and is trivial to undo. Ill-conditioning is about *unequal* stretching, which the condition number (and the SVD lesson) measures.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Where it shows up: linear layers, batches and attention scores
md: Linear layers are batched dot products ($XW^\top + b$). Attention scores are dot products between queries and keys ($QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$). Similarity search is a matrix-vector product. Vectors, dot products and matrix multiplication cover all three.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Classification end to end: logistic regression, boundaries and softmax
md: Logistic regression scores $z = w \cdot x + b$, squashes with the sigmoid, and learns from the gradient $(p - y)x$. Its decision boundary is the line $z = 0$. Softmax generalizes it to K classes with gradient $p - \text{onehot}(y)$. On separable data, weights grow without bound unless you regularize.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Measuring a model: metrics, thresholds and cross-validation
md: Choose metrics that match the costs: precision and recall for rare positives, AUC for ranking, RMSE or MAE in the units of $y$. Choose the threshold from the cost of each mistake. Use k-fold (stratified for classes) cross-validation when data are scarce, and still touch the test set once.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The forward pass: layers as matrix multiplies
md: Keep the cached values. The forward pass is not just for the prediction: the backward pass will reuse every $z^l$ and $a^l$ computed here, so frameworks store them.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Training a real network: an MLP on handwritten digits
md: Use the test set once. If you pick the number of epochs, the learning rate or the hidden size by looking at test accuracy, the test set has become a validation set and its score is no longer an honest estimate. Choose with the validation set, then report test.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency: race conditions and locks
md: "It is a single line of C" does not make it atomic, and `volatile` does not either: that C keyword only tells the compiler to really load and store the variable on every access instead of keeping it in a register. OSTEP's counter is declared `volatile int` and still loses updates.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Crash consistency: fsck and journaling
md: Write the pointed-to object before the object that points to it, and make the commit a single atomic write. Journaling turns three unordered writes into one all-or-nothing transaction, and recovery only has to read the log, not the whole disk.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Joint and marginal distributions, and the chain rule of probability
md: The joint table holds everything. Marginals are its row and column sums, conditionals are a row or column divided by its total, and the chain rule rebuilds the joint from one-variable conditionals.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
md: Entropy is average surprise under the truth, cross-entropy is average surprise under your model, and KL divergence is the gap. Training on cross-entropy minimizes KL from the data, which is maximum likelihood.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
md: 6ND counts useful model FLOPs, not wall-clock. Real hardware sustains only a fraction of its peak, so time and cost depend on utilization. And at long context lengths the attention term that 6N ignores stops being small. Serving a trained model costs about $2N$ FLOPs per generated token (forward pass only), which matters in lesson 7.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Why you need a test collection before you can say better
md: Relevance is judged against the **information need**, not the query words. A document that contains every query term can still be nonrelevant, and a document with none of them can be relevant. That is exactly why judgments must come from people and not from term matching.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Comparing systems honestly: judgment holes, variance, significance
md: By default trec_eval silently ignores queries for which a run retrieved nothing, so a system that crashes on hard queries can score higher. Pass -c to average over every query in the qrels, with missing queries scored 0.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine
md: Pooling a pretrained language model does not give you a good embedding model. BERT was never trained to make cosine meaningful; the training objective in the next lesson is what does that.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Why language models read subwords, not words or characters
md: A token is not a word. In GPT-2, " hello" (with its leading space) and "hello" are two different tokens with different ids, and many common words are split. Counting words is a poor estimate of token count.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Special tokens, chat templates and prompt boundaries
md: Special tokens are added by hand and matched before BPE, so only text you control should be allowed to produce them. Chat templates are just strings of special tokens and text. And the model sees ids, so prompt edges and spelling tasks inherit tokenization's boundaries.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm and dropout: train vs eval mode
md: BatchNorm and Dropout behave **differently in train and eval mode**. `model.train()` and `model.eval()` flip that switch for every such layer at once; forgetting either one is among the most common silent bugs in practice.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
lessonTitle: Greedy search on a proximity graph, and why ef matters
md: Greedy graph search has no guarantee of exactness on a real (non-Delaunay) graph. Even a large $ef$ can miss a neighbor if the graph has no path that improves toward it. Recall comes from how well the graph is built, which is the subject of the next two lessons.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Dependencies and transitive trees: code you never chose
md: Misconception: "I only use five packages." You use five packages plus everything they pull in. Count with `npm ls --all | wc -l` or `pip list` inside a fresh virtual environment, and you will usually find one to two orders of magnitude more.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: SBOMs: an ingredients list you can query when the alarm rings
md: An SBOM is a claim about contents, only as complete as the tool that wrote it. It lists what is present, not whether any of it is malicious, and an SBOM made from source can miss what the build pulled in. Generate it from the built artifact, sign it, and keep it with the artifact.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
md: The question is not whether synthetic data enter the loop, but whether real data stay in it. Keep the original human data, keep adding fresh real data, and treat synthetic data as an addition. Even then, a fixed share of mismatched synthetic data floors the error, so its quality matters as much as its quantity.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When a system call blocks: sleeping, short counts and EINTR
md: Retrying `EINTR` is right for `read` and `write`. For calls with a timeout (`poll`, `epoll_wait`, `nanosleep`), retrying with the original timeout restarts the clock, so a steady stream of signals could stretch the wait without limit. Recompute the time left before retrying.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Watching and restricting system calls: strace, faults and seccomp
md: Trust strace's counts more than its times. Tracing stops the program at every call, so `-c` and `-T` times are inflated, and calls served by the vDSO never appear at all (the cost lesson). Measure speed without strace, for example with `perf stat`, and use strace to learn what the program does.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Taming the tail: hedged requests and honest reporting
md: Honest tail reporting: record every request into a mergeable histogram (HdrHistogram or bucketed histograms), measure from intended start under a load plan, merge histograms rather than percentiles across machines, and report several high percentiles plus the max, with the sample count.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Inside the 5G core: service APIs, OAuth tokens, SEPP and slices
md: SEPP and OAuth protect only what passes through them. ENISA warned in 2018 that 5G risked "repeating history", and as long as networks still interwork with SS7 and Diameter for older phones and roaming partners, the old interfaces stay attack surfaces.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
